core: working definition of competitive advantage, attributed to OpenStax Introduction to Business section 11.2: a set of unique features of a company and its products perceived by the target market as significant and superior to those of the competition; also called a differential advantage; 'the factor that causes customers to patronize a specific firm and not the competition'

the classic sources of advantage named with one line and an original example each: cost, quality, speed, service, brand (the five-source framing folds OpenStax's product differentiation and brand-name material under quality and brand, and adds speed via the first-mover advantage)

sustainable versus temporary advantage: advantages erode because competitors copy what works; OpenStax warns a cost advantage may not offer a long-term advantage; 'sustainable' taught as hard to copy, not permanent
the value proposition: a promise of value stated by a company that summarizes how the benefit of its product or service will be delivered, experienced, and acquired (CFI definition), stated simply
advantage versus strategy: the edge (the result, visible in customer choices) versus the plan to build and defend it; business-strategy is a sibling topic, referenced only
finding your advantage as a general practice: market research finds customers, competitive analysis makes a business unique, combining them finds a competitive advantage (SBA)
the honest framing: advantage is earned daily, not owned; competitors copy in the background, so an advantage that is not maintained becomes a disadvantage
supporting: OpenStax's four-type taxonomy: cost, product differentiation, service differentiation, and niche competitive advantage
cost advantage mechanics: inexpensive raw materials, efficient operations, design for ease of manufacture, control of overhead
first-mover advantage: the edge gained by first introducing a product or service to market, building brand recognition and loyalty before other entrants (CFI)
CFI framing: competitive advantage as what sets a company apart in the eyes of its consumers, often called a 'protective moat'; strong, repeatable advantages create sustained success
SBA market-research questions: demand, market size, economic indicators, location, market saturation, pricing
value proposition as the statement of the edge in customer terms, distinct from a slogan

claims.claim: OpenStax's Introduction to Business (section 11.2) defines a competitive advantage — also called a differential advantage — as a set of unique features of a company and its products that are perceived by the target market(s) as significant and superior to those of the competition; it adds that competitive advantage is the factor that causes customers to patronize a specific firm and not the competition.

OpenStax names four types of competitive advantage: cost, product differentiation, service differentiation, and niche; a firm with a cost competitive advantage produces at lower cost than all competitors while maintaining satisfactory profit margins.

Advantages erode: OpenStax states that over time a cost competitive advantage may fail because other firms adopt the same technology and competing firms match low costs by using the same lower-cost suppliers, so a cost competitive advantage may not offer a long-term advantage; differential advantages (brand names, product reliability, service) tend to be more durable.

Corporate Finance Institute describes competitive advantage as the ways a company can produce goods or deliver services better than its competitors; it is what sets a company apart in the eyes of its consumers, is something that cannot be easily replicated, is often called a 'protective moat,' and strong, repeatable competitive advantages can create sustained success.

A value proposition is a promise of value stated by a company that summarizes how the benefit of the company's product or service will be delivered, experienced, and acquired; it specifies what makes the offering attractive, why a customer should purchase it, and how it is differentiated from similar offerings (CFI definition).

The first-mover advantage is an advantage gained by a company that first introduces a product or service to the market; it enables a company to establish strong brand recognition and product or service loyalty before other entrants arrive (CFI).

The U.S. Small Business Administration teaches that market research helps you find customers and competitive analysis helps you make your business unique; combining them is how a small business finds a competitive advantage, using questions about demand, market size, economic indicators, location, market saturation, and pricing.

The lesson's distinction between competitive advantage (the edge — the result visible in customer choices) and strategy (the plan to build and defend that edge) is its own teaching framing; OpenStax presents competitive advantage as an outcome discussed within its marketing-strategy section, and the business-strategy sibling topic owns the planning tools in depth.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many types of competitive advantage there are, and what to name them
positions: OpenStax names four types: cost, product differentiation, service differentiation, and niche.
General business writing often lists sources such as cost, quality, service, and brand, and separately treats first-mover speed as an advantage.

The lesson names five classic sources — cost, quality, speed, service, brand — as a simplified teaching framing, and explicitly names OpenStax's four-type taxonomy alongside it (quality and brand fold into product differentiation; speed rests on the first-mover advantage).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the five classic sources as its own framing for general-literacy readers, grounded in OpenStax for cost, quality (product differentiation), service (service differentiation), and brand (brand-name differential advantages), and in CFI's first-mover advantage for speed; OpenStax's four-type taxonomy is named in the lesson so the source-verified classification is not lost.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether any competitive advantage can be called sustainable
positions: OpenStax warns that cost advantages erode as rivals adopt the same technology and suppliers, and may not offer a long-term advantage, while differential advantages tend to last longer.
CFI holds that strong and repeatable competitive advantages can create sustained success for a business.
The lesson teaches 'sustainable' as hard to copy rather than permanent: brand, service, and quality outlast cost, but no advantage is immune to copying.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the honest note central: advantages erode, competitors copy what works, and 'sustainable' describes how hard an advantage is to copy, not a guarantee of permanence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a value proposition is a promise to customers or just a slogan
positions: CFI defines a value proposition as a promise of value stating how the benefit of the product or service will be delivered, experienced, and acquired.
Casual usage applies the term to any company tagline or mission-style statement.
The lesson uses the CFI definition and adds a common-mistake entry distinguishing the value proposition from a slogan.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the CFI definition: the value proposition is the promise of what the customer gets and why it is worth their money, not a slogan about the company.
